title: Ladki Bahin eKYC 2026: How to Do It, Status, Fix
meta_description: Ladki Bahin eKYC 2026: how to complete it on ladakibahin.maharashtra.gov.in, the annual June-July window, what to do if your account was removed.

hero.one_liner: How to complete your Majhi Ladki Bahin eKYC, what the annual window means, and how to fix the errors that get women wrongly removed from the list.

what_is_it: eKYC is the yearly check that confirms you are still a genuine Majhi Ladki Bahin beneficiary. You complete it with your Aadhaar number and an OTP.
It is mandatory. If you skip it, your monthly ₹1,500 stops, and your name can be removed from the beneficiary list.
You do it on the official Maharashtra portal with your Aadhaar and a one-time password. No agent and no payment are ever needed.
Doing it yourself, on the official site, also keeps your details safe. The whole process is meant to take only a few minutes once your Aadhaar and mobile are linked.
eligibility: You are already an approved Majhi Ladki Bahin beneficiary.
Your Aadhaar is linked to a mobile number to receive the OTP.
Your Aadhaar is seeded to your bank account so payments can arrive.

eligibility_filters.notes: eKYC is for existing Majhi Ladki Bahin beneficiaries. Annual verification to keep the ₹1,500 monthly payment.

extra_sections.heading: 💡 Why eKYC matters for your ₹1,500
content: eKYC is how Maharashtra confirms each year that you are still a real, eligible beneficiary. It is not a one-time formality.
Skip it and the monthly ₹1,500 stops. After the deadline, accounts that did not complete it can be removed from the list entirely.
This is why the eKYC window matters so much. Completing it on time is the single thing that keeps your payment running.
Think of eKYC as renewing a pass. The scheme has lakhs of names, and the state uses this yearly check to make sure each ₹1,500 is going to a real, eligible woman.
It also catches errors and duplicates. In the last round the state found lakhs of names that should not have been on the list, which is part of why the check is now strict.
For you, the takeaway is simple. Treat the eKYC window like a bill that must be paid on time, because missing it costs you the monthly money.
The state has said clearly the scheme will continue, with a large budget set aside. So the money is there; eKYC is simply the gate you walk through to keep receiving your share.
Some women ignore eKYC thinking one missed month is harmless. In reality a missed verification can drop you from the list, and getting back on is far harder than staying on.

extra_sections.heading: 🪪 How to do Ladki Bahin eKYC online

steps.title: Open the official portal
steps.desc: Go to ladakibahin.maharashtra.gov.in. Use only the official site, never a third-party link, for eKYC.

steps.title: Open the eKYC section
steps.desc: Find the eKYC option on the home page and enter your Aadhaar number.

steps.title: Verify the OTP
steps.desc: An OTP is sent to the mobile number linked to your Aadhaar. Enter it to authenticate.

steps.title: Confirm your details
steps.desc: Answer the verification questions carefully and submit. You get a confirmation on screen and by SMS.

extra_sections.heading: 🏢 Can you do eKYC offline?
content: Not everyone has a smartphone or a stable connection, and that is fine. You can complete eKYC offline with help.
Visit an Anganwadi centre, a Setu Suvidha Kendra, or a Common Service Centre with your Aadhaar card and your Aadhaar-linked mobile. The worker there helps you do the same Aadhaar and OTP step.
This route is genuinely free at government centres. If anyone at a private shop asks for money to do your eKYC, walk away and use an Anganwadi instead.
Carry your original Aadhaar and, if you have it, your application acknowledgement. The centre will not need much else for a routine yearly check.
The offline route is also the safest for older women or anyone unsure with phones. A trusted Anganwadi worker doing it in front of you beats a stranger doing it for a fee.
Take a family member along if you can. A second person helps you read the verification questions carefully and remember what was submitted.
Government centres handle thousands of these, so the staff know the common errors. That experience alone can save you a rejected attempt.

extra_sections.heading: 📋 What to keep ready before eKYC
content: A few minutes of preparation saves a lot of frustration. Keep your Aadhaar card and your application details within reach before you start.
Make sure the mobile that receives your OTP is the one linked to your Aadhaar, and that it has signal and some balance. Many failed attempts are simply an OTP going to an old number.
Know the answer to the family government-service question in advance. Decide it calmly at home, not in a hurry on the portal.
If your name has changed after marriage, make sure your Aadhaar and bank reflect the same name. A mismatch between the two is a quiet but common cause of failure.
It also helps to have your bank account number and the linked mobile noted somewhere. If the portal asks you to confirm a detail, you will not be hunting for it.
Do the eKYC when you have ten quiet minutes, not while cooking or travelling. Rushing is exactly when the wrong option gets ticked.
If you completed eKYC in an earlier round, the yearly one feels familiar. The screens are the same, so a little memory from last time speeds it up.

extra_sections.title: The one question that wrongly removed lakhs of women
extra_sections.content:
During verification, a confusingly worded Marathi question asks whether anyone in your family is in government service. Over 24 lakh women ticked the wrong option here.

Read this question very slowly. Answering it wrong can wrongly mark you ineligible and block your payment.

If you are not sure, get help from an Anganwadi worker or CSC centre before you submit, not after.

extra_sections.heading: 📅 When is the eKYC window in 2026
content: eKYC runs on an annual cycle. After the earlier deadline closed on 30 April 2026, the next mandatory verification window is expected to open around June to July 2026.
The government reopens this window roughly the same time each year, usually for about two months. Because exact dates shift, always confirm the current window on the official portal.
The safest habit is to complete eKYC as soon as the window opens. Leaving it to the last week is when the portal is most overloaded.
The first round ran from September 2025 and was extended four times before closing on 30 April 2026. That history tells you the government does give extra time, but you should never count on it.
From now on, plan for a regular yearly window rather than a single event. Each year the verification reopens, usually for around two months.
Watch the official portal and local Anganwadi announcements as June begins. The moment the window is confirmed open, do your eKYC and stop worrying about it for the year.
One more thing about timing. The four extensions last year happened because so many women were left out, not because the rule was relaxed.
So while extra time may come again, the smart move is to act in the first two weeks. People who wait for an extension are the ones who lose out when none arrives.

extra_sections.heading: 🔁 First eKYC vs the yearly re-check
content: Your very first eKYC confirmed you into the scheme. The yearly re-check is lighter, but just as compulsory.
Each year the state reopens the window to confirm you are still eligible and still alive in the records. Nothing about your bank or Aadhaar should change if your details are stable.
If your mobile, bank, or address changed during the year, fix those first. An out-of-date detail is the most common reason a yearly re-check suddenly fails.
Set a simple yearly reminder on your phone for June. Treating it as a fixed annual task means you never scramble at a deadline again.
A small comfort: if your details have not changed all year, the yearly check is quick and usually passes the first time.
Problems mostly hit women whose mobile, bank, or Aadhaar details drifted out of sync. Keeping those three matching is the whole secret to a painless re-check.

extra_sections.heading: ✅ Before you start eKYC, check these
qualify: You are an approved Ladki Bahin beneficiary
Your Aadhaar is linked to your current mobile number
Your Aadhaar is seeded to your bank account
You know whether anyone in your family is a government employee
disqualify: Aadhaar not linked to any working mobile number
Bank account not seeded with Aadhaar
Relying on an unofficial website or agent

extra_sections.heading: 🔧 Portal not opening or OTP not coming
content: When everyone rushes to the portal near a deadline, the server slows down and pages may go blank. This is traffic, not a problem with your application.
Try again in early morning or late at night when fewer people are online. The same eKYC link works at any hour.
If the OTP does not arrive, the usual cause is that your mobile number is not linked to your Aadhaar. Update it at an Aadhaar centre, then try eKYC again.
If the page loads blank or freezes, do not refresh repeatedly or open it on many devices. That adds to the load and can lock you out temporarily.
Close the page, wait a while, and try once in a quiet hour. A single clean attempt at 6 am works better than twenty attempts at 8 pm.

extra_sections.heading: 🔁 More on portal and OTP problems
content: If your OTP still fails after your mobile is Aadhaar-linked, the link may be to an old number you no longer use. Updating it at an Aadhaar centre fixes this for good.
If nothing works for days even in quiet hours, it is worth visiting an Anganwadi. They sometimes have a smoother connection and can complete it for you on the spot.
Clear your browser or try a different one if a page keeps breaking. A stale page sometimes holds an old error and a fresh one loads cleanly.
And do not pay anyone who promises to skip the queue. There is no paid fast lane; the same free portal serves everyone.
Many women also share one phone in a household. Make sure the eKYC OTP goes to the number actually linked to your Aadhaar, not a relative’s phone.

extra_sections.heading: 📉 Why missing eKYC is so costly
extra_sections.title: accounts were removed after the last deadline
extra_sections.desc: After the April 2026 deadline closed, about 68 lakh accounts that had not completed eKYC were removed from the list. Around 1.88 crore verified women kept receiving their ₹1,500. The gap between those two numbers is what one missed eKYC can cost.

extra_sections.heading: 🚪 My account was removed: what now
content: After the April 2026 deadline, around 68 lakh accounts that did not complete eKYC were closed. If yours was removed, do not panic and do not pay any agent.

If you were removed by mistake, for example from the wrongly answered government-service question, call helpline 181 with your Application ID. Many genuinely eligible women had their payments restored after review.
Visit the nearest Women and Child Development office, Anganwadi centre, or CSC. They can check your case and guide a correction where one is allowed.
First, confirm it is really removed and not just a delayed payment. Enter your Aadhaar in the eKYC section: if it sends an OTP, your name is still on the list.
If you see the message that the Aadhaar is not in the list, that is when you act. Note your Application ID and the exact message before you call.
When you call 181 or visit the office, be calm and specific. Say whether you think it was the government-service question or a genuine eligibility issue, because the fix differs for each.
Keep any SMS you received during earlier eKYC rounds. Proof that you tried or completed it before can help your case during a review.
Act quickly once you confirm removal. Review windows and correction modules are open only for limited periods, so the sooner you raise it, the better your chances.

extra_sections.heading: ⚠️ Mistakes that cost women their payment
content: The biggest mistake is waiting for the last day. The portal is slowest then, and if a problem appears you have no time to fix it.
The second is trusting an agent or an unofficial website. They may take your money, your OTP, or both, and your eKYC still will not be valid.
The third is assuming silence means success. Always wait for the on-screen confirmation and the SMS, and note them down as proof.
Finally, never share your OTP with anyone who calls claiming to help. The government never asks for your OTP over a phone call, and sharing it can empty your account.
Another quiet mistake is changing your bank account and not updating it everywhere. If the scheme still points to your old account, the money goes nowhere useful.
Keep one stable Aadhaar-seeded account for the scheme. Consistency across Aadhaar, mobile and bank is what keeps payments smooth year after year.
In short, do it early, do it on the official site, and confirm it went through. Those three habits prevent almost every eKYC problem women face.

extra_sections.heading: 💸 eKYC done but payment still not arriving
content: Completing eKYC confirms your eligibility, but the money only reaches an Aadhaar-seeded bank account. These are two different links.
Check your Aadhaar to bank seeding status and, if it is not active, visit your bank to complete it. Payments resume once the seeding is in place.
After that, check status on the portal under your earlier applications, and look for the credit in the Aadhaar-linked account, not a different one.
A useful mental model is two doors. eKYC opens the first door that says you are eligible, and Aadhaar bank seeding opens the second door that lets the money actually walk in.
Many women clear the first and forget the second. They see eKYC complete on screen, assume all is done, and then wonder why the account stays empty.
Ask your bank to confirm your account is Aadhaar-seeded and set to receive DBT. This one visit resolves most after-eKYC payment delays.
If the credit shows in your statement with a PFMS or government reference, that is your confirmation. Save a screenshot for your own records.
If a month genuinely goes missing even after eKYC and seeding are fine, raise it through the official grievance route rather than waiting silently.
Note the month, your Application ID, and your last successful payment date. Specific details get cases resolved far faster than a vague complaint.

extra_sections.heading: 📨 After eKYC: what happens next
content: Once eKYC is confirmed, you do not need to do anything else until next year's window. Keep the confirmation SMS safe.
Your monthly ₹1,500 continues to the Aadhaar-seeded bank account as before. If a month is missed, check status on the portal before assuming anything is wrong.
There is no separate certificate to collect and no office visit needed if everything went through online. Simple is the goal here.
Treat the confirmation SMS like a receipt. If a question ever comes up about whether you completed eKYC, that message is your proof.
Beyond that, no news is good news. A quiet account that keeps crediting ₹1,500 each month means your eKYC did its job.

extra_sections.title: The one-minute yearly habit that protects your ₹1,500
extra_sections.content:
Every June, do three things. Check that your Aadhaar is linked to your current mobile, confirm your bank account is Aadhaar-seeded, and complete eKYC as soon as the window opens.

Done early, the whole thing takes a few minutes. Done late, it becomes the stressful scramble that costs lakhs of women their payment each year.

extra_sections.text: eKYC and bank seeding are not the same thing. You can finish eKYC perfectly and still get no money if your Aadhaar is not linked to the bank account that should receive it.

faqs.question: How do I do Ladki Bahin eKYC online?
faqs.answer: Open ladakibahin.maharashtra.gov.in and go to the eKYC section. Enter your Aadhaar number, verify the OTP sent to your linked mobile, and submit the verification.

faqs.question: Is Ladki Bahin eKYC mandatory?
faqs.answer:
Yes. eKYC is mandatory and must be completed in each annual window.

If you skip it, your monthly ₹1,500 stops and your account can be removed.

faqs.question: What is the Ladki Bahin eKYC last date in 2026?
faqs.answer: The earlier deadline of 30 April 2026 has passed. The next annual verification window is expected around June to July 2026, so confirm the exact date on the official portal.

faqs.question: My account was removed after the deadline. Can I get it back?
faqs.answer: If you were removed by mistake, call helpline 181 with your Application ID or visit a Women and Child Development office. Many wrongly removed women had payments restored, though genuinely ineligible accounts stay closed.

faqs.question: The eKYC portal is not opening. What should I do?
faqs.answer: This is usually heavy traffic near the deadline, not a fault with your application. Try again early morning or late night when the portal is less busy.

faqs.question: I am not getting the eKYC OTP. Why?
faqs.answer: The usual reason is that your mobile number is not linked to your Aadhaar. Update your mobile at an Aadhaar centre, then try the eKYC again.

faqs.question: I completed eKYC but the payment has not come. Why?
faqs.answer: eKYC confirms eligibility, but money only reaches an Aadhaar-seeded bank account. Visit your bank to complete Aadhaar seeding, then check the linked account.

faqs.question: Do I have to pay anyone for eKYC?
faqs.answer: No. eKYC is completely free on the official portal. Never pay an agent, and never share your OTP with anyone.

faqs.question: How do I check if my name is still on the Ladki Bahin list?
faqs.answer: Go to the eKYC section and enter your Aadhaar number. If you get an OTP, your name is on the list, but if you see a message that the Aadhaar is not in the list, call 181 with your Application ID.

faqs.question: How often do I need to do Ladki Bahin eKYC?
faqs.answer: eKYC is an annual requirement. You need to complete it once each year in the verification window to keep receiving the monthly payment.
